lead: An integrated optical waveguide is a narrow strip of high-index material on a chip that holds light in two directions: vertically by the layer stack and sideways by the strip edges. Many such guides, with splitters, couplers and modulators, share one substrate as a photonic integrated circuit. The guide is a planar slab cut to a finite width, so its design reuses the slab V number, and the effective index method turns the two-dimensional problem into two slab problems. Only a few universities teach this topic in detail.
prereq: You need: the slab V number and mode count from Electromagnetic mode theory; modes in planar guides.

blocks.text: A planar guide confines light only across its thickness. To route light on a chip it must be confined sideways as well, which needs a core of finite width w as well as thickness t. The core has index n₁; the substrate below and the cladding around it have lower indices (here both n₂). Light is held wherever the core meets lower-index material.

items: Strip (or raised strip) guide: the core layer is etched into a strip standing on the substrate, with air or a deposited cladding over it. The sidewalls give a strong index step.

Ridge or rib guide: the core is only partly etched, leaving a thin slab on each side of a raised ridge; the side confinement is weaker, which keeps the guide single-mode at larger widths and lowers sidewall scattering.
Channel (buried or embedded) guide: the core is a rectangle buried in cladding on all sides, made by diffusion or ion exchange into the substrate or by depositing cladding over a strip.

blocks.text: Names vary between books: many use 'channel waveguide' for any guide that confines in two directions, strips and ridges included, and others reserve it for the buried core. Say which you mean when you answer.

sections.h3: Single-mode check and the effective index method

blocks.text: The thickness direction is a slab, so the slab V of the mode-theory chapter applies, with the same full-thickness convention:

blocks.where: t is the core thickness and λ the vacuum wavelength in the same unit; √(n₁² − n₂²) is the NA of the index step, here a measure of contrast rather than a launch angle. A symmetric stack is single-mode across its thickness when V < π. In an asymmetric stack (air above) even the fundamental mode has a cutoff, and the single-mode range moves up by that amount.

blocks.text: The effective index method handles the width. Step 1: solve the vertical slab (thickness t) for its mode; its effective index neff,1 lies between n₂ and n₁. Step 2: treat the guide, seen from above, as a lateral slab of width w with core index neff,1 and side index n₂ (for a buried channel), and apply the slab rule again with Vw = (2πw/λ)√(neff,1² − n₂²). The guide is single-mode only if both checks pass.

Because n<sub>eff,1</sub> is below n₁, the lateral contrast is weaker than the material contrast, so a guide is often much wider than it is thick before a second lateral mode appears. A high-contrast platform such as silicon on silica holds light in a core about 0.22 µm thick and 0.5 µm wide and allows bends of a few micrometres radius; low-contrast glass guides are several micrometres across and need millimetre bends.

Photonic integrated circuits combine guides with Y-branch splitters, directional couplers, ring resonators, arrayed waveguide gratings and modulators on one chip. A Mach–Zehnder modulator splits the guided light into two arms, shifts the phase in one arm with an applied voltage, and recombines them so that the output intensity follows the voltage (see Optical modulators and Mach-Zehnder devices). Practical limits are loss from sidewall roughness, coupling loss to a fiber whose mode is far larger than the chip's, and different behaviour for the two polarizations.

examples.question: A buried channel guide has core thickness t = 0.5 µm, width w = 2 µm, n₁ = 1.50 and n₂ = 1.45 all round, used at λ = 1.55 µm. Find the NA of the index step and V for the thickness direction, and decide whether the thickness direction is single-mode.
steps: The stack is symmetric (n₂ above and below), so the limit is π = 3.142. V = 0.778 < π: one mode across the thickness.
examples.answer: NA = 0.384 and V = 0.778, well below π, so the thickness direction is single-mode.

examples.question: Continue with the effective index method. The vertical slab of the first example, solved numerically, has TE₀ effective index n<sub>eff,1</sub> = 1.4564. Check the width direction and estimate the guide's effective index, given that the lateral slab's fundamental-mode solution is 1.4514.
steps: V<sub>w</sub> = 1.106 < π, so only one lateral mode: the guide is single-mode in both directions.
Widest single-mode strip: w < λ/(2 × 0.1364) = 1.55/0.2728 = 5.7 µm.
Guide effective index 1.4514: it lies between n₂ = 1.45 and n<sub>eff,1</sub> = 1.4564, as it must, because the second confinement pushes more of the field into the cladding.
examples.answer: V<sub>w</sub> = 1.11 < π, so the 2 µm guide is single-mode (it stays so up to about 5.7 µm wide); its effective index is about 1.451.

traps: Do not use the fiber limit 2.405 for a slab or strip. With V built on the full thickness, a symmetric slab is single-mode for V < π (half-thickness books write π/2).
The thickness check says nothing about the width. A guide can be single-mode vertically and multimode sideways; check the width with the effective index.
In the lateral step use n<sub>eff,1</sub> from the vertical slab, not n₁; using n₁ overstates the lateral contrast and the mode count.
Effective indices obey n₂ < n<sub>eff</sub> < n₁, and each added confinement lowers n<sub>eff</sub> a little more.
Keep t, w and λ in one unit; t/λ and w/λ must be pure numbers.

quiz.q: Name three kinds of integrated optical waveguide.
quiz.a: Strip (raised strip), ridge or rib, and buried (embedded) channel guides.

quiz.q: Why is a planar slab not enough on a chip, and what does the strip add?
quiz.a: A slab confines light only across its thickness, so light spreads sideways. Cutting the core to a finite width adds index steps at the sides, confining light in both transverse directions so it can be routed.

quiz.q: A symmetric stack has t = 0.6 µm, n₁ = 1.48, n₂ = 1.46 at λ = 1.3 µm. Find V for the thickness and decide if it is single-mode.
quiz.a: NA = √0.0588 = 0.2425; 2πt/λ = 2.900; V = 2.900 × 0.2425 = 0.703 < π, so single-mode across the thickness.

quiz.q: For the stack of the worked example (n₁ = 1.50, n₂ = 1.45, λ = 1.55 µm), find the largest thickness that is single-mode vertically.
What is the effective index of a mode, and where must it lie?
quiz.a: n<sub>eff</sub> = β/k₀, the index a plane wave would need to travel at the mode's phase velocity; it lies between the cladding and core indices because the mode runs partly in each.

quiz.q: A guide has V = 0.7 across its thickness but is 8 µm wide, with the lateral step of the second worked example. Is it single-mode?
quiz.a: No. V<sub>w</sub> = (2π × 8/1.55) × 0.1364 = 4.42, which is above π, so a second lateral mode is guided; the guide is single-mode only below about 5.7 µm width.

quiz.q: Why do silicon guides allow much tighter bends than glass guides?
quiz.a: Silicon (n about 3.5) on silica (1.44) is a very large index step, so the mode is held tightly and does not radiate at a bend of a few micrometres; a glass guide with a step of 0.01 to 0.05 holds its mode weakly and radiates unless the bend radius is large.

beyond: Not for the exam. Silicon photonics builds transceivers for data centres from silicon strip guides, germanium detectors and silicon modulators on standard chip lines. Silicon nitride guides give lower loss over a wider band, and thin-film lithium niobate gives fast, low-voltage modulators. Search next for silicon-on-insulator waveguides, the effective index method, and grating couplers for fiber-to-chip coupling.
